why: Darwin argues by claim and instance: a principle, then grouse, plums, wolves, clover, cabbages, a plot of turf. So the lens leads with a ledger of claims, each tied to its examples. The chapter also describes, line by line, a diagram that this plain-text edition does not contain; the lens rebuilds it from the prose, keeping what the text states apart from what the rebuild infers. A map, a cast of informants and a tally of Darwin's numbers complete it.

lenses.title: Claims and their instances
lenses.why: Natural history argues by example, so each claim is shown with the cases that carry it.

cards.claim: Natural selection is the preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious ones.

src.q: This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.

examples.label: Neutral variation is left to fluctuate (polymorphic species)

src.q: Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.

cards.claim: Nature can select on any internal organ; man selects only visible characters, for his own good.

src.q: Man can act only on external and visible characters: nature cares nothing for appearances, except in so far as they may be useful to any being.

examples.label: Long- and short-beaked pigeons fed the same food

cards.claim: Selection can act at any age, because characters are inherited at the corresponding age.

src.q: natural selection will be enabled to act on and modify organic beings at any age, by the accumulation of profitable variations at that age, and by their inheritance at a corresponding age.
